issues.legal_issue: The classification of displaced persons and their rural property for verification and compensation under the rehabilitation scheme does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged rules governing claims for rural buildings as discriminatory, arguing that the scheme treated urban and rural residents, rural landowners and owners of rural houses, and recipients of different kinds of land allotments differently.
The scheme treated rural property and urban property separately, and treated a rural building differently depending on its value and whether the claimant had received agricultural land.
The distinctions and thresholds reflected policy decisions made in the course of intergovernmental arrangements concerning evacuee property.

The rehabilitation scheme provided rural allottees with houses or, where houses were unavailable, building sites and grants; it also provided rehabilitation grants in specified circumstances where rural property claims were rejected.
issues.conclusion: The challenged classification was not arbitrary, had a reasonable relation to the objective of equitable rehabilitation, and did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality; the petition was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The equality guarantee permits classification when it rests on an intelligible differentia relevant to the subject and bears a reasonable nexus to the object sought to be achieved. The classification must be assessed in light of the exceptional circumstances and the need for equitable rehabilitation and distribution of available property. The Court relied on Rule 57 and Rules 97 and 97-A of the rules under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, and noted recognition of the intergovernmental agreement in Article 31(5)(b)(iii) of the Constitution. No earlier cases are cited.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns rehabilitation rules that distinguish rural from urban property and classify rural buildings by land allotment and value, and those distinctions reflect intergovernmental policy while rural claimants receive or may receive alternative housing support, the classification is constitutionally valid.
